_readme: Single source of truth for every robot/field number. PLACEHOLDER values are marked in _placeholders. Edit, save, then press F5 in the sim (or restart) to reload. Units are in the key names.
_placeholders: turret.servo_speed_deg_per_s, levers.speed_deg_per_s (depends on the servos you buy)
levers.front_deploy_sign / back_deploy_sign (flip if a lever swings the wrong way)
drivetrain.loaded_speed_fraction / strafe_efficiency / accel limits (tune against the real robot)
field.* (check the BIOBUZZ field drawings); heights and flower/hive behaviour are guesses
intakes.* and shooter.* (speeds, capacity, how balls are held and released)

field._layout_note: The floor plan comes from data/field_layout.json (BEE simulator, manual TU02). The numbers below are GUESSES for things that file does not give.
field._flower_note: The flower is the real CAD (cad/field/flower.glb, am-5855). Heights are measured from it, above the tiles: the middle ring a nectar rests on, the scoring volume (between the middle ring and the top ring) and the top ring. Pollen stand on the tile inside the floor ring and are taken out under the middle ring; balls go in through the top ring. flower_radius_in + flower_lever_reach_in = how close to the flower's centre a deployed lever must be to wedge a pollen out (GUESS).
field._hive_note: The hive is a seesaw on top of the A-frame (models in cad/field/). Pivot height 43.95 in and tilt 30 deg are the BEE simulator's values (from the game manual); the frame CAD's axle holder agrees to within an inch. It tips when the WEIGHT in the raised cell reaches hive_tip_weight_g. The manual gives no number; the BEE simulator uses a random 88 to 112 g, and the team's rule of 8 pollen is 100 g. A nectar (26.5 g) counts a bit more than two pollen (12.5 g). Three nectar (79.5 g) start in each raised cell, so the FIRST tip of a match needs only 2 pollen; after that an empty cell needs 8 pollen, or 4 nectar. Each tip scores 20 points and lets the alliance's humans put one more nectar into their loading zone.
field._april_tag_note: From the official AprilTag art (ftc-resources.firstinspires.org, 2027 field): every hive cell has a cluster of four 36h11 tags on a 17 x 5 in sticker on its underside. FTC SDK 12.0 reports each cluster as one detection whose pose points at the centre of the cell's opening.

pollen._note: Size, weight and bounce are read from data/game_elements.json when it exists; these are the fallback values.
pollen._air_note: Flight through the air. drag_coefficient 0.5 is typical for a smooth ball (BEE uses the same). Spin: the top shooter wheel's surface moves faster than the flywheel's, so the pollen leaves with topspin and dips. spin_efficiency is how much of the ideal spin it really gets (PLACEHOLDER) and lift_coefficient_max caps the Magnus lift (PLACEHOLDER). Set spin_efficiency to 0 to switch spin off.
pollen._squeeze_note: PLACEHOLDER. squeeze_force_n = how hard the ball pushes back when the shooter wheels squash it by the full amount (pollen 16.8 mm, the team's 1.69 cm). Estimated from a hollow polyethylene shell of the ball's weight (about 45 N pollen, 100 N nectar); the soft 35A wheels give way too, so the real figure is probably lower. MEASURE IT: squash a ball that far on a kitchen scale (45 N = 4.6 kg). squeeze_loss_fraction = share of the squashing work that does not spring back.

nectar._note: The bigger, heavier ball (red / blue). Size, weight and bounce come from data/game_elements.json (3.6 in, 26.5 g); these are the fallback values and the flight numbers. Being heavier for its size it loses less speed to the air than a pollen.
nectar._squeeze_note: PLACEHOLDER, see pollen._squeeze_note. A nectar is squashed 37 mm by the shooter wheels (the team's 3.69 cm).

intakes._note: One motor per intake + its feeder. Front = side A (plain Intake in the CAD), back = Intake-Mirrored. Both feeders lead into the shared neck under the shooter.
intakes._push_note: PLACEHOLDER: how hard a feeder pushes a ball into the shooter wheels (5 N = about half a kilo). Only matters when the wheels cannot grip a ball by themselves (see shooter.wheel_grip).

shooter._note: Two motors on one flywheel. A ball waiting at the neck is launched when the gate is open, its intake/feeder motor runs AND the flywheel is spinning.
shooter._mirrored_note: Found on the real robot: the two shooter motors face each other, and the left one is the mirrored one, so the code has to reverse shooterLeft. If the code reverses neither, the two fight and the flywheel does not turn; if it reverses the wrong one, the flywheel spins backwards. The sim shows both mistakes.
shooter._gate_note: ASSUMPTION: something holds pollen at the neck until you want to shoot (a gate/stopper servo). Without one, running a feeder with the flywheel spinning fires straight away. Position > 0.5 = open.
shooter._compression_note: The gap between the two pairs of green wheels is 54.3 mm in the CAD (wheel_gap_mm). A 71.1 mm pollen is squashed 16.8 mm and a 91.4 mm nectar 37.1 mm on the way through: the team's 1.69 and 3.69 (centimetres). The intake squashes them 0.39 and 2.39 cm.
shooter._speed_note: Motors are the goBILDA 312 rpm Yellow Jacket with the gearbox removed: 6000 rpm free speed, 1:1 to the 4 in flywheel; the 3 in top wheel is geared 2.25x faster. Surface speeds at full power: 31.9 m/s (flywheel) and 53.9 m/s (top wheel), average 42.9 m/s. exit_speed_fraction = ball speed / flywheel surface speed = 1.34 (the average of the two wheels) x 0.6 efficiency. The 0.6 is a PLACEHOLDER for slip and compression losses: measure a real shot and adjust it. That gives about 25.5 m/s at full power, so real shots use roughly a fifth of full power.
shooter._flywheel_note: What the motors have to spin, from the CAD: two 0.125 kg flywheel weights (71 mm discs) and two 4 in 35A compliant wheels on the motor shaft, plus two 3 in wheels turning 2.25x faster. Wheel weights are PLACEHOLDERS (weigh one). Together that is about 7.4e-4 kg m^2 at the shaft; at a shooting speed of 1300 rpm it stores about 7 joules. A pollen takes about 0.4 J out of it (speed dips 4 percent), a nectar about 1.5 J (11 percent). The weights are what keep that dip small.
shooter._motor_note: Two bare goBILDA Yellow Jacket motors: 0.144 N m stall torque each (1.47 kg cm), falling to zero at 6000 rpm. velocity_control true = the code holds the speed (RUN_USING_ENCODER or setVelocity): the hub gives full voltage whenever the wheel is slow, so it is back to speed in a few hundredths of a second. false = plain setPower with RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER: recovery takes over a second and a stream of shots gets weaker and weaker. A Java OpMode decides this itself by the mode it sets on the shooter motors.
shooter._grip_note: PLACEHOLDERS. wheel_grip = friction between the green wheels and a ball (soft 35A rubber on smooth polyethylene, roughly 0.6 to 1.0). The wheels pull a pollen in by themselves with a grip of 0.5 or more; a nectar meets them at a steeper slant and needs 0.77, or else a push from the feeder (intakes.feeder_push_n). slip_energy_factor: the wheels spend about twice the energy the ball ends up with, the rest is rubbing heat.
shooter._stream_note: Rate of fire. shot_interval_s is the shortest gap between two balls through the wheels; feeder_transit_s (under intakes) is how fast the feeders bring the next one. How much each ball slows the flywheel is worked out from the weights above. Below min_speed_fraction_to_shoot the feeder does not offer a ball to the wheels at all.
shooter._hood_note: MEASURED from cad/shooter_min.glb and cad/shooter_max.glb (2026-11). The shooter has two wheels: a 4 in flywheel and a 3 in top wheel carried by the hood, which swings around the flywheel axle. Pollen leaves through the gap between them, at right angles to the line joining the two wheel centres. That line is 22.7 deg above horizontal with the hood at its start and 43.8 deg at its end, so the shot leaves at 67.3 deg (start) down to 46.2 deg (end) above the floor. Assumes the shooter sits on the robot at the same tilt as in cad/Robot.glb; uncertainty about 2 deg. Servo 0 = flattest (hood at its end), servo 1 = steepest (hood at its start).
shooter._parts_note: For the moving shooter parts, from models/measurements.json (turret frame, +x = shooting direction): where the flywheel axle and the top wheel axle are, and the angle of the line between them in the CAD export (hood at its start).
shooter._exit_note: Where pollen leaves, in the turret frame: about 0.39 m above the floor, from the CAD.

robot._size_note: Measured from the CAD by tools/process_cad.mjs (see models/measurements.json). This box is what collides with walls.

Measured from the new CAD (2026-11) by tools/process_cad.mjs, with the levers folded up. The team quoted a frame width of 438.214 mm and a chassis length of 334.075 mm without intakes; the collision box needs the outermost size, so it uses the CAD.
robot._start_note: PLACEHOLDER start pose: near the red alliance wall, facing across the field.

drivetrain._inverted_note: PLACEHOLDER. true = positive power on that motor drives its wheel BACKWARDS, because of how the motor is mounted. On most mecanum robots the left side is like this, which is why real code calls setDirection(REVERSE) on the left motors. Used only when Java code drives the robot.
drivetrain._track_note: Measured between the mecanum wheel centres in both CAD exports (390.9 mm). The team quoted 335.169 mm, which must be measured between something else (the frame rails?); the simulator needs wheel centre to wheel centre.

turret._continuous_note: continuous = true: the turret can turn all the way round, with no end stops (needs a continuous or multi-turn servo and a way to keep the wires from winding up). false: limited to servo_range_deg through the gears.
turret._home_note: Where the shooter points when the turret servo is centred (position 0.5), counter-clockwise from the robot's right side. 90 = straight ahead, which is how the new CAD is exported.
turret._speed_note: How fast the servo itself turns; the turret gets 15/70 of it. goBILDA dual mode servos on the hub's 5 V: Speed (25-3) about 545 deg/s = 117 deg/s at the turret; Torque (25-2) about 240 deg/s = 51 deg/s at the turret. At 6 V (servo power module): 667 and 300 deg/s. Set to the Speed servo, the one recommended for shooting on the move; put 240 here to try the Torque servo.

levers._note: Servo position 0 = stowed (upright, as in the CAD), 1 = deployed. Pivots are in the robot frame (+x right, +y up, -z forward, metres), from models/measurements.json.
levers._servo_note: Each lever is turned by TWO servos, one at each end of its bar: first list = front lever, second = back lever. The two servos of a pair face each other, so one of them (mirrored_servos) turns the opposite way for the same position: the code has to reverse it, or the pair fights instead of moving (the HUD then says so).
levers._cad_pose_note: How far the levers are folded out in the CAD export (0 = upright, 90 = flat), from models/measurements.json. The new CAD has them at 138 deg, i.e. past flat and pointing down.
levers._angles_note: From the team: the levers rest at 15 deg (default) and go to 138 deg to work the flowers. 0 = straight up, 90 = flat.

camera._note: The main camera: an Arducam (USB webcam) on the shooter, looking where it shoots, read in code through the FTC VisionPortal + AprilTagProcessor. The sim does not process images: it works out which AprilTags are in view from where the robot and turret are. position_m is in the turret's frame (+x = shooting direction, +y up) and comes from the CAD ('Camera <1>' on the shooter); mount_pitch_deg (tilted up 45 deg) is from the team. tag_size_in is measured off the official sticker art. PLACEHOLDERS: the field of view (depends on the Arducam model and lens), max range and viewing angle. The chassis also carries a second camera and two Huskylens as helpers; they are not simulated yet.
camera.name: Webcam 1

odometry._note: Two dead-wheel pods read as encoders. Offsets measured from the CAD (models/measurements.json). Wheel size and ticks are PLACEHOLDERS (goBILDA pod: 32 mm, 2000 ticks/rev).
odometry._pinpoint_note: The real robot reads its two goBILDA 4-Bar pods (32 mm wheel) through a goBILDA Pinpoint odometry computer on an I2C port. A Java OpMode gets it with hardwareMap.get(GoBildaPinpointDriver.class, "pinpoint"). The simulated one is perfect: no wheel slip and no drift.

java._note: Running real OpModes. teamcode_dir: folder with your OpMode .java files; empty = the java/teamcode folder of this project. You can point it at your real TeamCode folder. command: how to start Java (a JDK 11 or newer).

realism._note: Real-world imperfections, so the sim is not kinder than the robot. ALL of these are GUESSES at typical FTC values: measure your robot and change them. Set enabled to false for a perfect robot. shot scatter = how much one shot differs from the next (spread of speed in percent, of direction in degrees). turret_delay_s = how late the servo starts to follow a command; turret_backlash_deg = play in the 15:70 gears. speed_* = how the robot knows its own speed for shooting on the move (odometry): late, a few percent long or short, and noisy. pose_error_in = how far off the robot's idea of its place on the field is.

driver._tolerance_note: With auto-aim, pollen are fed only while the flywheel is within this fraction of the speed the shot needs. Bigger = faster stream, less accurate.
driver._descent_note: Automatic hood: among the shots that reach the cell, it takes the one needing the least flywheel speed whose pollen is still coming down at least this steeply when it arrives. Bigger = steeper, more lobbed shots.
driver._moving_note: Shooting on the move. A ball keeps the robot's speed when it leaves, so with lead_moving_shots the turret aims ahead by (robot speed x flight time) and the hood/flywheel are worked out as seen from the moving robot. Fire is held while the turret is more than shoot_aim_tolerance_deg from where it should point (it falls behind when the robot drives past the hive or turns faster than the turret can).
